📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 BIG PICTURE

You can read Korean by tonight. Seriously. Hangul (한글) was designed by King Sejong in 1443 specifically to be learnable in a day or two. It is the most scientifically-designed writing system on Earth.

Why this is genuinely easier than you think

Hangul is not like Chinese characters. There are only 40 letters total (24 base + 16 combinations). Each letter represents a single sound. Once you know them, you can read any Korean word — even ones you don't understand. Pronunciation becomes a recognition task, not a memorization task.

Compare this to English: "tough", "through", "though", "thought" all share spelling patterns and pronounce differently. Hangul has none of that. Spelled how it sounds. Sounded how it's spelled.

How syllables stack into blocks

Unlike English where letters sit in a line (h-e-l-l-o), Hangul letters stack into syllable blocks. Each block is one syllable. Three letters might fit in one block. This is what gives Korean writing its distinctive square shape.

Look at this:

한 + 국 = 한국

"han" + "guk" = "Hanguk" (Korea)

Each block is one beat. The block 한 has three letters stacked: ㅎ (h) + ㅏ (a) + ㄴ (n) = "han". The block 국 has three letters: ㄱ (g) + ㅜ (u) + ㄱ (k) = "guk". Two blocks = two syllables = "Han-guk".

🎓 HISTORY MOMENT

Before Hangul, Koreans wrote with Chinese characters that didn't fit the language well. Only scholars could read or write. King Sejong created Hangul so commoners could be literate. The official document explaining it (Hunminjeongeum, 1446) literally says: "Even a stupid man can learn this in 10 days." High praise from a king. 600 years later, you're proving him right.

Realistic expectations for your first week

  • Today (Ch 1): Recognize 14 consonants. Some will stick instantly; others will feel awkward. Normal.
  • Day 2 (Ch 2): 10 vowels. Now you can read basic syllables.
  • Day 3 (Ch 3): Compound sounds. You'll start reading restaurant signs and Instagram posts.
  • Day 4 (Ch 4): Final consonants and pronunciation rules. The "hard" chapter — most people skip it, then regret it. Don't skip it.
  • Day 5+: Numbers, speech levels, real phrases. Hangul becomes background; you start using the language.

Goal for Chapter 1: By the end, you'll recognize all 14 basic consonants and have your first few words you can read aloud. Tap the 🔊 buttons constantly. Use the 🎙️ button to practice saying them. Don't worry about perfect pronunciation yet — you're building recognition, not fluency.

Your first Korean syllable, right now

Tap to hear it:

That's ㄱ (g) + ㅏ (a). One consonant, one vowel, one syllable. That's it. Now you've read your first Korean character.

Ready? Let's meet the 14 consonants.

The 14 basic consonants

These are the building blocks. Each one has a name, a sound, and a shape that often hints at how your mouth makes the sound. We'll learn them in 4 groups so it's not overwhelming.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Group 1 — The "feels familiar" four: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㅁ

These map cleanly to English sounds. Start here.

Mnemonic trick:

  • ㄱ looks like a gun barrel — gun = g
  • ㄴ looks like a foot stepping forward — n
  • ㄷ looks like a closed door — door = d
  • ㅁ looks like a mouth/box — mouth = m

Group 2 — The "needs practice" four: ㅂ ㅅ ㅈ ㅎ

Familiar sounds but the shapes need repetition.

Mnemonics:

  • ㅂ looks like a bucket holding water — bucket = b
  • ㅅ looks like a slingshot — slingshot = s
  • ㅈ like ㅅ with a hat — the "j" sound
  • ㅎ a person wearing a hat — the breathy h

Group 3 — The "aspirated" four: ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ

"Aspirated" means with extra breath. Hold your hand in front of your mouth — saying these should create a puff of air, like saying "Peter" emphatically. They look like their unaspirated cousins with an extra line added.

💡 PATTERN TO NOTICE

See the pairs? ㄱ→ㅋ (g→k, add line). ㄷ→ㅌ (d→t, add line). ㅂ→ㅍ (b→p, redesigned). ㅈ→ㅊ (j→ch, add hat). The "aspirated" cousin always looks similar with extra strokes. This isn't coincidence — Sejong literally designed them this way. Pattern-thinking pays off in Hangul.

Group 4 — The two strange ones: ㄹ and ㅇ

ㄹ is genuinely tricky. It's not the English R (which rolls back) and not the English L (which sticks). It's a single flap — like the "tt" in American "butter". Practice: 라, 라, 라 — quick, light tongue tap.

ㅇ is the weirdest letter in the alphabet — at the start of a syllable it's silent. It's just a placeholder so the vowel has something to attach to. (At the END of a syllable, it becomes "ng" like in "sing" — we'll get to that in Ch 4.) So 아 (a-with-silent-ㅇ) is just pronounced "a". 오 is "o". 우 is "u". The ㅇ does nothing.

All 14 at a glance

Take a screenshot of this. Tap each one. Say it out loud.

CharNameSoundHear it

ㄴ니은 (nieun)n
ㄷ디귿 (digeut)d (initial), t (final)
ㄹ리을 (rieul)r/l flap
ㅁ미음 (mieum)m
ㅂ비읍 (bieup)b (initial), p (final)
ㅅ시옷 (siot)s

Spend 5 minutes tapping through all 14. You don't need to memorize them perfectly today — just expose your eyes and ears. Tomorrow we add vowels and you can read real words.

Position changes pronunciation

Here's the first thing that trips up English speakers: some Korean consonants change their sound depending on where they appear in a syllable.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Specifically: ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅈ sound like "g, d, b, j" at the START of a syllable, but become "k, t, p" at the END. (ㅈ at end becomes t too.)

LetterAt startAt endExample
ㄱgk
ㄷdt
ㅂbp

You don't need to think about this — your mouth will do it naturally because saying "guk" with a hard final k is easier than ending on a soft "g". Just be aware: 국 isn't "goog" — it's "gook" (with a clipped k).

The ㅇ chameleon

ㅇ is silent at the start, but says "ng" at the end. Same letter, two jobs.

  • 아 = "a" (ㅇ is silent, just supporting the vowel)
  • 강 = "gang" (ㅇ at the end = "ng" sound)

Try it:

Why this design is brilliant

King Sejong didn't just invent random shapes. The consonant shapes were designed to mimic the position of the mouth/tongue when making each sound.

  • ㄱ — back of tongue raised (g/k sounds): the bent shape mimics tongue against the soft palate
  • ㄴ — tongue tip touching upper teeth (n): the shape is the tongue's profile
  • ㅁ — closed lips (m): the closed box shape is the mouth seen from front
  • ㅅ — air rushing between teeth (s): the angled shape suggests airflow
  • ㅇ — open throat (silent/ng): the open circle = open mouth

If you've ever wondered "why is Korean so easy to learn to read compared to Chinese?" — this is why. The script is a schematic of speech itself.

Practice: read these syllables out loud

Tap each one, listen, then try to say it. The 🎙️ button records your voice and shows what was heard.

If your match scores are low, don't panic. Speech recognition is finicky — try saying it more slowly and clearly. Often "70% match" is actually correct pronunciation that the recognizer misheard.

A phrase you'll actually use

You don't have all the vowels yet, but here's a phrase you can already read. You'll use this constantly:

Break it down: 감사 (gam-sa, "thanks") + 합니다 (ham-ni-da, formal verb ending). Together: "I do thanks" → "I thank you."

💡 KOREAN ETIQUETTE

When you say 감사합니다, bow slightly. About 15 degrees from the waist — not a full bend, just a respectful nod that extends to the upper body. This is automatic in Korean culture. With his parents/elders, the bow matters as much as the words. Practice the bow as you say the phrase — they go together.

More casual situations: just 감사해요 (polite) or 고마워 (casual, only with friends/peers/your boyfriend).

The 3-level version of "thank you"

This is your first taste of speech levels. Same meaning, three different forms based on who you're talking to.

반말 — CASUAL (boyfriend, close friends, kids)
해요체 — POLITE (most adults, default)

Or:

하십시오체 — FORMAL (his parents, elders, work)
⚠️ FOR YOUR SITUATION SPECIFICALLY

To his parents: Always 감사합니다 (formal). Never 고마워 — that would feel disrespectful, almost like a child being rude.

To your boyfriend: 고마워 (casual) once you're comfortable. Using 감사합니다 to him would feel weirdly distant, like you're treating him as a stranger.

To his siblings (his age or younger): 고마워 if they've okayed casual speech (very common between in-law siblings of similar age once introduced). If older sibling and you're not super close yet: 고마워요.

End of chapter — quick self-check

Before moving to Chapter 2, you should be able to:

  • ✓ Recognize all 14 consonant shapes (no need to memorize names)
  • ✓ Know which 4 consonants are "aspirated" (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ)
  • ✓ Understand that ㅇ is silent at start, "ng" at end
  • ✓ Read a few simple syllables aloud
  • ✓ Say 감사합니다 (formal thank you) with appropriate bow

If any of those feel shaky, re-read the relevant section or take the quiz to find your weak spots. Chapter 2 adds vowels — that's when you really start reading.

One last thing: this stuff sticks faster than you'd guess. Even if it feels foreign now, in 3 days the shapes will start auto-recognizing. Your brain is good at this.

화이팅! (hwaiting — "you can do it" — the most Korean word in Korean)

The 10 basic vowels

Now the magic happens. Consonants alone don't make syllables — they need vowels. Today you learn the 10 basic vowels and then you can read.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Korean vowels come in two flavors based on shape:

  • Vertical vowels (a tall line with marks on the side): ㅏ ㅑ ㅓ ㅕ ㅣ
  • Horizontal vowels (a flat line with marks above/below): ㅗ ㅛ ㅜ ㅠ ㅡ

This matters for how they stack with consonants — vertical vowels go to the RIGHT of the consonant, horizontal vowels go BELOW. You'll see this in Section 2.

The 5 "plain" vowels — learn these first

⚠ THE TRICKY ONES

ㅓ (eo) and ㅡ (eu) trip up English speakers because we don't have these exact sounds.

ㅓ: think British "hot" — the "o" is more like "uh". Or imagine the vowel in "duh".
ㅡ: spread your lips wide (like smiling) and say "uh". It's NOT the "oo" in moon — that's ㅜ.

If you confuse them, you'll say wrong words. The word 어 ("oh!" exclamation) ≠ 으 (just a sound when surprised, almost grunt-like).

The 4 "y-versions" — same vowel but starts with a "y" glide

Korean has a clever pattern: take a plain vowel, add a SECOND short stroke, and it becomes the "y" version of that vowel.

Plain→ Y-versionSoundHear
ㅏ (a)ㅑ (ya)"ya" as in yacht
ㅓ (eo)ㅕ (yeo)"yuh" — yawning sound
ㅗ (o)ㅛ (yo)"yo" as in yo-yo
ㅜ (u)ㅠ (yu)"yu" as in you

Pattern check: ㅡ (eu) and ㅣ (i) don't have y-versions. Just memorize the 4 above.

Tap each vowel. Say it. Repeat 5x. Vowels are the soul of Korean — getting them right is more important than perfect consonants.

Vowel contrast: ㅑ adds a y-glide to ㅏ — ya vs a; the extra stroke means the y sound at the start. That is how the two vowels are different from each other.

How syllables stack: the block system

Time to combine consonants + vowels into actual syllable blocks. There are 3 layouts based on the vowel shape:

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Layout 1 — Vertical vowel: consonant LEFT, vowel RIGHT

Vertical vowels: ㅏ ㅑ ㅓ ㅕ ㅣ ㅐ ㅒ ㅔ ㅖ

ㄱ + ㅏ = 가

"g" + "a" = "ga"

The consonant ㄱ sits on the LEFT, the vowel ㅏ sits to its RIGHT, together they form the block 가.

More examples — tap each:

Layout 2 — Horizontal vowel: consonant TOP, vowel BOTTOM

Horizontal vowels: ㅗ ㅛ ㅜ ㅠ ㅡ

ㄱ + ㅗ = 고

"g" + "o" = "go"

The consonant ㄱ sits on TOP, the vowel ㅗ sits BELOW.

Layout 3 — With a final consonant (batchim) — bottom layer

When a syllable has a final consonant, it goes UNDERNEATH the whole thing. (We cover batchim in detail in Chapter 4, but you'll see it now.)

ㄱ + ㅏ + ㅁ = 감

"g" + "a" + "m" = "gam" (persimmon)

Write your name in Hangul

Find your name's syllables in Korean approximations. Examples:

  • Natasha → 나타샤 (Na-ta-sha)
  • Mike → 마이크 (Ma-i-keu) — Koreans add a vowel to lonely consonants
  • Sarah → 사라 (Sa-ra)
  • David → 데이비드 (De-i-bi-deu)
💡 ENGLISH NAMES IN KOREAN

Korean syllables MUST be consonant+vowel (with optional final consonant). So if your name has consonant clusters (like "Christ" — 3 consonants in a row), Koreans break them up by inserting the vowel ㅡ (eu).

"Christmas" becomes 크리스마스 (keu-ri-seu-ma-seu — 5 syllables!). It looks long but each syllable is short. Loanwords from English follow this pattern.

Y-vowels in real words

Now use the y-vowels (ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ) in actual vocabulary. These add a quick "y" sound at the start of the vowel.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Compare these pairs — same consonant, vowel without vs with the y glide:

Without YWith YDifference
ㅏ → ㅑ adds 'y'
ㅓ → ㅕ adds 'y'
ㅗ → ㅛ adds 'y'
ㅜ → ㅠ adds 'y'

Useful words with y-vowels

One of your most-used words: 요

The syllable 요 (yo) at the END of a verb makes it polite. We'll learn this properly in Chapter 6 (speech levels), but here's a preview:

반말 — CASUAL ending
해요체 — POLITE (just add 요!)

See? Adding 요 makes any sentence polite. It's the single most useful syllable in Korean for politeness.

One more example with 요:

반말 — CASUAL
해요체 — POLITE

You'll hear and say 좋아요 constantly. It's the Korean equivalent of "good" / "I like it" / "sounds good" / 👍.

Pronunciation anchor: ㅑ sounds like English ya, as in yacht.

The 5 double consonants — "tense" sounds

Korean has a 3-way distinction English doesn't: plain / aspirated / tense. You already know plain (ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅅ ㅈ) and aspirated (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ — with extra breath). Now meet the tense ones — same letter doubled, pronounced with extra muscle tension and no breath.

PlainAspiratedTenseSound
ga (soft) / ka (breathy) / kka (tense, no breath)
da / ta / tta
ba / pa / ppa
—sa / (no aspirated) / ssa
ja / cha / jja
💡 HOW TO MAKE "TENSE" SOUNDS

Tense sounds are the trickiest for English speakers. Think of how you'd say "Peter" emphasizing the P with no breath release — your throat is tight, no air comes out. That tension is the "tense" quality.

Practical test: hold a tissue in front of your mouth.
• Aspirated (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ) = tissue moves a LOT (puff of air)
• Plain (ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ) = tissue moves a little
• Tense (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ) = tissue should NOT MOVE at all (no air, just muscle tension)

Why this matters — wrong tension = wrong word

Distinguishing plain/aspirated/tense is critical. Example: ㄱ vs ㅋ vs ㄲ all change meaning:

One sound change = completely different word. Don't worry — your ear catches up fast. Most beginners get this wrong for weeks, then it suddenly clicks.

Common words with tense consonants

Tense-consonant minimal pair: 달 (dal) = moon, 딸 (ttal) = daughter — the doubled ㄸ is the tense sound, and it changes the meaning entirely.

The 11 compound vowels

Compound vowels are combinations of the basic vowels you already know. The patterns are systematic — once you know how they combine, you can predict the sound.

The "-i" family (base vowel + ㅣ): ㅐ ㅒ ㅔ ㅖ

Add ㅣ (i) to a vowel and you get a more closed/forward sound.

⚠ HONEST TRUTH ABOUT ㅐ vs ㅔ

In modern spoken Korean, ㅐ and ㅔ sound nearly identical. Most Korean speakers under 50 cannot reliably distinguish them by ear. You still need to know both for SPELLING (the words are spelled differently), but don't stress about hearing the difference — even native speakers don't.

The "w-" family (ㅗ or ㅜ + vowel): ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ

These all start with a "w" glide. ㅗ-based ones use the "wa-" sound; ㅜ-based ones use "wo-" / "wi-".

LetterSoundBuilt fromHear
ㅘwaㅗ + ㅏ
ㅙwaeㅗ + ㅐ
ㅚoeㅗ + ㅣ
ㅝwoㅜ + ㅓ
ㅞweㅜ + ㅔ
ㅟwiㅜ + ㅣ

The notorious ㅢ

ㅢ is famously tricky. It's pronounced 3 different ways depending on context:

  • As the first syllable of a word: say "eu-ee" quickly — almost like "wee" but starting with ㅡ. Example:
  • Inside or end of a word: usually just "ee" (like ㅣ). Example:
  • As the possessive particle: pronounced "e" (like ㅔ). Example:

You don't need to memorize this now. Just know: when you see ㅢ and it sounds different than expected, this is why.

The vowel pairs that even Koreans confuse

These vowel pairs sound nearly identical in modern Korean. You'll see them spelled differently in writing but pronounced the same way in speech. Knowing this saves you frustration.

ㅐ vs ㅔ — basically the same

Once different ("ae" vs "e"), now merged in modern Seoul Korean to roughly the same sound (between English "e" and "a" in "bed").

Different words, almost identical pronunciation. Context tells you which.

ㅙ vs ㅚ vs ㅞ — all pronounced like "we"

These three are functionally indistinguishable in modern speech. All sound like English "way" or "we".

You'll need to know which one each word uses for spelling, but listening, they're the same.

ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ (the y-vowels)

These remain clearly distinct. Don't confuse them.

vs"ya" vs "yuh" — clear difference
vs"yo" vs "you" — clear difference

For listening: Don't sweat ㅐ/ㅔ or ㅙ/ㅚ/ㅞ — context will clarify.

For speaking: Pronounce them all roughly the same — natives won't notice or care.

For typing/writing: You'll have to learn which word uses which spelling. Use Anki-style repetition.

What is batchim (받침)?

받침 means "support" — and that's exactly what these are: a final consonant that supports the bottom of a syllable block.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

You've already seen batchim in earlier chapters. Now we understand them properly.

한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ

The ㄴ at the bottom is the batchim — pronounced "n" at the end of "han".

Almost any consonant can be a batchim

All 14 basic consonants + the 5 double consonants + some double-batchim combinations (ㄳ ㄵ ㄺ etc.) can appear as final consonants. That's a lot of possibilities — but here's the kindness: they all collapse into only 7 actual pronounced sounds.

Korean has a rule called "representative pronunciation" (대표음). No matter what consonant is written as batchim, only one of 7 sounds actually comes out.

Where batchim sits in the block

Batchim ALWAYS goes on the bottom of the block, regardless of whether the vowel is vertical or horizontal:

밥= ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ"bap" — rice/food. Final ㅂ on bottom.
꽃= ㄲ + ㅗ + ㅊ"kkoch" → pronounced "kkot" (representative pronunciation!) — flower
물= ㅁ + ㅜ + ㄹ"mul" — water. Vertical vowel ㅜ on top, batchim ㄹ on bottom.

The 7 final consonant sounds

This is the key rule of Korean pronunciation. Memorize this table — it explains 90% of why spoken Korean differs from written.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Pronounced asWritten as (any of these)Example
ㄱ (k)ㄱ, ㅋ, ㄲ
ㄴ (n)ㄴ
ㄷ (t)ㄷ, ㅌ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅎ
ㄹ (l)ㄹ
ㅁ (m)ㅁ
ㅂ (p)ㅂ, ㅍ
ㅇ (ng)ㅇ

The collapsing — why it happens

Look at the "ㄷ (t)" row above. It says ㄷ, ㅌ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅎ — seven different letters all collapse to the same "t" sound when they're at the END of a syllable.

So:

  • is spelled with ㅊ at the end, but pronounced "kkot" (with t).
  • is spelled with ㅅ at the end, but pronounced "ot" (with t).
  • is spelled with ㅌ at the end, but pronounced "kkeut" (with t).

Why? Korean ends syllables CLEANLY — no sustained sounds. ㅈ at the end can't keep buzzing, so it cuts off as a hard t.

💡 PATTERN MEMORY TRICK

Group by mouth position:

k-family (back of mouth): ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ → all sound like ㄱ at end
t-family (tip of tongue): ㄷ ㅌ ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅎ → all sound like ㄷ at end
p-family (lips): ㅂ ㅍ → both sound like ㅂ at end

The simple consonants (ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅇ) keep their own sound at the end. The complicated ones collapse to their simplest form.

Liaison: when consonants jump syllables

This is the rule that makes spoken Korean sound DIFFERENT from how it's written, and trips up every learner.

Rule: When a syllable ends in a batchim AND the next syllable starts with ㅇ (silent), the batchim "jumps" to the next syllable.

Example: 음악 (music)

Written: 음 + 악 — "eum" + "ak"

You'd expect to hear: "eum-ak"

What you actually hear:

The ㅁ at the end of 음 jumps over to become the start of 악, which had only the silent ㅇ. So instead of "eum-ak", we hear "eu-mak".

Another example: 한국어 (Korean language)

Written: 한 + 국 + 어 — "han" + "guk" + "eo"

Liaison effect:

Why this matters

When you start listening to Korean, you'll hear sounds and try to find them in your dictionary — but they won't be there because of liaison. You have to mentally "un-link" what you hear back into the written form.

Practice — listen and notice the liaison

Other pronunciation shifts (preview — don't memorize yet)

Korean has more rules — consonant assimilation, ㅎ weakening, nasalization. You don't need to memorize them now. Your ear will pick them up from listening.

Examples:

  • 국물 (broth) — written "guk-mul", pronounced
  • 입학 (admission) — written "ip-hak", pronounced

Just know these shifts exist. As you listen more, your ear catches them automatically.

Sometimes you'll see TWO consonants stacked at the bottom of a block. These are double batchim (겹받침).

Rule: When followed by a vowel (next syllable starts with ㅇ), BOTH consonants get used — the first stays, the second jumps to the next syllable. When followed by a consonant or at end of word, only ONE is pronounced.

You don't need to master this now. Just recognize: if you see two consonants stacked under a vowel, only one usually gets pronounced.

Korean has TWO number systems

This catches every learner off guard: Korean uses two completely different sets of numbers depending on what you're counting. You need both. Get this wrong and you sound like a 5-year-old.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
  • Sino-Korean numbers (일이삼사…) — borrowed from Chinese. Used for math, dates, money, minutes, addresses, phone numbers.
  • Native Korean numbers (하나둘셋…) — original Korean. Used for ages, hours (on the clock), counting objects and people.

Don't worry — the rules are clear. Let's learn Sino-Korean first since it's more regular.

Sino-Korean numbers 1-10

#HangulRomanizationHear

1일il
2이i
3삼sam
4사sa
5오o
6육yuk
7칠chil
8팔pal
9구gu
10십sip

Building bigger Sino-Korean numbers

Once you know 1-10, you can build any number up to 99 with a simple pattern:

  • 20 = 2-10: 이십 (i-sip)
  • 30 = 3-10: 삼십 (sam-sip)
  • 21 = 2-10-1: 이십일 (i-sip-il)
  • 45 = 4-10-5: 사십오 (sa-sip-o)
  • 99 = 9-10-9: 구십구 (gu-sip-gu)

Big units:

  • 100 = 백 (baek)
  • 1,000 = 천 (cheon)
  • 10,000 = 만 (man)
  • 100,000,000 = 억 (eok)
⚠ THE 만 (10,000) TRAP

English groups by thousands (1,000 / 1,000,000). Korean groups by 10,000s (만/억). When you see a price like 50,000 won, Koreans don't say "50 thousand" — they say "5만" (o-man, "five ten-thousands"). This takes practice.

Examples:
• 10,000 won = 만 원 (man won)
• 50,000 won = 5만 원 (o-man won)
• 100,000 won = 10만 원 (sip-man won — "ten ten-thousands")

The native system. Only goes up to 99 — for higher numbers, switch to Sino-Korean.

The "counter form" — critical

When you put a Native Korean number IN FRONT of a counter word (like "year old" or "people"), numbers 1-4 and 20 change shape slightly:

  • 하나 → 한 + counter (e.g., 한 살 = "1 year old")
  • 둘 → 두 + counter (두 명 = "2 people")
  • 셋 → 세 + counter (세 개 = "3 items")
  • 넷 → 네 + counter (네 시 = "4 o'clock")
  • 스물 → 스무 + counter (스무 살 = "20 years old")

The other numbers (5-19, 30+) stay the same. Only those four change.

20-99 in native Korean

Each tens digit has its own word (unlike Sino-Korean which builds "2-10, 3-10"). Bring back your flashcards:

20: 스물30: 서른 (seoreun)40: 마흔 (maheun)50: 쉰 (swin)

Building combos: 서른다섯 (seoreun-daseot) = 35. 아흔아홉 (aheun-ahop) = 99.

Above 100, switch to Sino-Korean. Nobody counts to 100 in native Korean.

When to use which system — the rules

This is where things get clearer. Each category has a clear rule.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Use SINO-KOREAN for:

CategoryExamples

Phone numbers공일공-삼사오육-칠팔구공 (010-3456-7890)
Dates (month/day/year)오월 십일 (May 10th), 이천이십육년 (year 2026)
Minutes & seconds삼십 분 (30 minutes), 십 초 (10 seconds)
Addresses & floor numbers오 층 (5th floor)
Math, prices, grades이 더하기 삼은 오 (2 + 3 = 5)

Use NATIVE KOREAN for:

CategoryExamples
Age스물다섯 살 (25 years old)
Hours (clock time)세 시 (3 o'clock)
Counting people두 명 (2 people)
Counting general objects한 개 (1 item)
Counting most things다섯 잔 (5 cups)

The most important counters

Counters are like "pieces of paper" — you can't just say "3 paper", you have to say "3 SHEETS of paper". Korean uses counters for EVERYTHING. The counter follows the number.

  • 개 (gae) — general objects (1 apple, 3 books, etc.) — DEFAULT counter when unsure
  • 명 (myeong) — people (1 person, 5 people)
  • 분 (bun) — people (RESPECTFUL — use for elders/strangers)
  • 살 (sal) — years of age
  • 시 (si) — o'clock (hours)
  • 분 (bun) — minutes (same syllable as the people counter — context disambiguates)
  • 잔 (jan) — cups/glasses (of drink)
  • 병 (byeong) — bottles
  • 마리 (mari) — animals (1 dog, 2 cats)

The cardinal beginner mistake

Using Sino-Korean for age. If you say "스무살" you're 20. If you say "이십 살" you sound like you're trying really hard but got it wrong — like saying "I am twenty years of age" too formally and incorrectly. Native speakers will smile, correct you. It's fine. But now you know.

⚠ KOREAN AGE WORKS DIFFERENTLY

Until 2023, Koreans calculated age differently — adding 1 year at birth and 1 more on every Lunar New Year. So you could be "27 international, 28 Korean." In June 2023, Korea officially switched to international age. But many older people (your boyfriend's grandparents, anyone over 50) still casually use the old "Korean age" in conversation. If his grandma asks 몇 살이에요? ("how old are you?") and gets a different number than your passport says, this is why.

Age uses NATIVE numbers: twenty years old is 스무 살 — saying 이십 살 (Sino twenty) marks you as mixing the number systems; ages, hours, and counting things take native numbers. What happens if you mix them? You instantly sound like a textbook instead of a speaker — natives notice.

Or you can say (반 = half).

"What time is it?"

하십시오체 — FORMAL

Dates

Dates use Sino-Korean throughout. Format: year → month → day (BIG to SMALL).

May 10, 2026 =

Months: just say the Sino-Korean number + 월 (wol = month). January = 일월, February = 이월, ..., December = 십이월.
Watch out for June and October: instead of 육월 it's 유월 (yuwol), and instead of 십월 it's 시월 (siwol). Two exceptions — irregularities for easier pronunciation.

Money — won (원)

Korea uses won. No coins below 1,000 won (~$0.75) are common. Prices look big but the math is simple once you remember to group by 10,000s (만).

Asking someone's age politely

Korean culture is age-aware. Knowing someone's age changes how you speak to them. Common ways to ask:

반말 — only with peers/younger
해요체 — polite default
하십시오체 — formal/elders

NEVER use 몇 살이에요? with his parents or older relatives. Use 연세가 어떻게 되세요? — note the special word 연세 (yeonse) which is the honorific form of "age."

Saying YOUR age

Note: 스물 changes to 스무 before 살. So 25 = 스물 + 다섯 = 스물다섯 살 (the 스물 stays as 스물 because it has 다섯 after it, not 살 directly).

Irregular months: June is 유월 (yuwol), NOT 육월 — the ㄱ drops; October similarly is 시월. Two exceptions worth memorizing cold — when you say the month of June, always yuwol. The months run January through December as Sino number + 월, and these two drop a consonant. Distractor traps: yukwol keeps the ㄱ (wrong), and inventions like yeowol or myuwol are not months at all — yuwol is the only correct form.

The 3 speech levels you actually need

Korean technically has 7 speech levels but most modern speakers use 3. You need all 3. Each one matches a different relationship.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
반말 (banmal) — CASUAL

Who: Close friends, kids, your boyfriend, siblings/cousins your age or younger

Form: Plain verb stem + 아/어 (e.g., 가, 좋아, 먹어)

Feel: Warm, intimate, equal. Inappropriate with new people, elders, strangers.

해요체 (haeyoche) — POLITE

Who: Most adults you don't know well — shop staff, peers at work, strangers, your boyfriend's same-age friends

Form: Add 요 to the casual form (가요, 좋아요, 먹어요)

Feel: Friendly, respectful, not stiff. The SAFE DEFAULT. When in doubt, use this.

하십시오체 (hasipsioche) — FORMAL

Who: His parents, elders (especially grandparents/aunts/uncles), bosses, formal contexts, public announcements

Form: Verb stem + (스)ㅂ니다 (갑니다, 좋습니다, 먹습니다)

Feel: Formal, respectful, slightly distant. The proper level for ceremony and important first impressions.

When each level is right — common scenarios

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

Scenario 1: Meeting his mom for the first time

Use 하십시오체. Bow when greeting. Don't relax to 해요체 even if she's warm.

Scenario 2: Boyfriend asks how your day was

Use 반말. He's your boyfriend — formality would create distance.

Scenario 3: Ordering coffee from a barista

Use 해요체. Friendly but appropriate.

Scenario 4: His older sister introduces herself

Use 해요체. She's older — but not an "elder." Wait for her to suggest 반말 down the road.

The 4 cardinal mistakes

  1. Using 반말 with elders. This is the #1 sin. Saying 안녕 (casual hi) instead of 안녕하세요 (polite) to his mom would be a major faux pas.
  2. Using 하십시오체 with your boyfriend. Comes across cold or even sarcastic — like calling him "Sir." He'd ask what's wrong.
  3. Mixing levels mid-sentence. Pick one level and stick with it for the entire sentence. Switching mid-sentence sounds nervous or confused.
  4. Going TOO formal "to be safe." Using 하십시오체 in a casual coffee shop would make the barista uncomfortable. 해요체 is the universal safe default.

The "default safe" level

해요체 is your safe default for any new person who isn't a clear elder. It's friendly, respectful, not stiff. If unsure, use 해요체. The worst outcome is being a bit too polite — never a major offense.

⚠ DON'T DOWNSHIFT WITHOUT PERMISSION

In Korean culture, the OLDER/HIGHER-STATUS person decides when 반말 is okay. Don't relax to 반말 with his older siblings, cousins, or coworkers until they explicitly invite it. They'll usually say or . Until then, stay polite.

Speaking to young children — even strangers’ children — uses 반말: age, not familiarity, licenses the casual level downward.

How to switch — the verb endings

The "level" of a Korean sentence is determined entirely by how the verb ends. Once you know the patterns, you can convert any sentence between levels.

The three ending forms

LevelEnding patternExample: 가다 (to go)
반말verb stem + 아/어 (drop 다 from dictionary form)
해요체verb stem + 아요/어요 (add 요 to the casual)
하십시오체verb stem + (스)ㅂ니다

The 아 vs 어 rule

For 반말 and 해요체, do you use 아 or 어 after the stem? Look at the last vowel of the stem:

  • If the vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, use 아 (or 아요).
  • If the vowel is anything else, use 어 (or 어요).
  • If the stem ends in 하, use 해 (or 해요).
Verb (dictionary form)Stem vowel반말해요체하십시오체
가다 (to go)ㅏ → 아가가요갑니다
오다 (to come)ㅗ → 아와와요옵니다
먹다 (to eat)ㅓ → 어먹어먹어요먹습니다
마시다 (to drink)ㅣ → 어마셔마셔요마십니다
하다 (to do)special해해요합니다
보다 (to see)ㅗ → 아봐봐요봅니다

Notice the vowel contraction: 오 + 아 = 와 (not 오아), 보 + 아 = 봐 (not 보아). These contractions are standard.

💡 SHORTCUT THINKING

In practice: most learners memorize the 해요체 form of each verb (가요, 먹어요, 마셔요) first. Then:
• Drop the 요 → you have 반말
• Replace the ending with -(스)ㅂ니다 → you have 하십시오체

You don't need to think about ㅏ/ㅗ rules consciously — you'll absorb them by exposure.

The 하십시오체 (formal) pattern

Two rules:

  • If verb stem ends in a vowel (가-, 마시-, 보-): add ㅂ니다 → 갑니다, 마십니다, 봅니다
  • If verb stem ends in a consonant (먹-, 좋-, 듣-): add 습니다 → 먹습니다, 좋습니다, 듣습니다

For questions: change 다 to 까 → 갑니까? 먹습니까? 좋습니까?

Switching mid-conversation

You'll often need to switch levels in real life. Example: you're hanging out with your boyfriend (반말) and his mom walks in (suddenly 하십시오체). This is normal — Koreans do it constantly.

The trick: finish your current sentence in whatever level, then switch at the next sentence. Don't try to switch mid-sentence — sounds awkward.

Hello & goodbye — the variations

"Hello" in Korean has 3 levels (matching speech levels) and "goodbye" splits into 2 forms based on who's leaving. Let's get all of it.

안녕 literally means "peace/wellness." You're asking "Are you well?" — even though it's used like "hello."

Goodbye — two versions: who's staying vs going

This is unique to Korean. There's a different goodbye depending on whether YOU'RE leaving or THEY are.

SituationWhat you say

What honorifics actually do

Honorifics (높임말, nopimmal — "elevated speech") are SEPARATE from politeness levels (반말/해요체/하십시오체). They do a different job.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
  • Politeness levels raise your relationship with the LISTENER (the person you're talking TO).
  • Honorifics raise the SUBJECT of the sentence (the person you're talking ABOUT).

The two can combine independently. You can be polite to one person while honoring another. Example:

Imagine you're talking to your friend (peer — use 해요체) about her grandma (someone to be honored):

Notice:

  • The ending 세요 is polite (해요체) — appropriate for your friend listening
  • The -시- infix in 읽으세요 honors grandma (the subject)
  • The particle 께서 (instead of 이) further elevates grandma

존댓말 vs 높임말 — common confusion

  • 존댓말 (jondaetmal) = polite speech (the levels 해요체 and 하십시오체). What you do to your LISTENER.
  • 높임말 (nopimmal) = honorific speech (-시-, special verbs, special particles). What you do to the SUBJECT.

In casual usage these terms are often conflated. Don't sweat the distinction — just know that "raising" can happen at two levels.

His friends your ageNo
ChildrenNo
⚠ THE BOYFRIEND'S PARENTS WRINKLE

When you're alone with your boyfriend, you might say "your dad called" casually:


But when you're talking to HIS PARENTS about each other, honorifics are mandatory. Even talking to his MOM about his DAD requires honorifics on the dad. The honorific stays whenever a respected elder is the SUBJECT, regardless of who you're talking TO.

His mom will protest ("아유, 뭘 이런 걸…" — "oh, why this kind of thing…") — that's the ritual response, expected. You smile, give a small bow, that's it.

His parents and grandparents

This chapter is about getting titles right. Korean family titles are dense — way more granular than English. Calling someone the wrong title isn't just awkward, it can be a real misstep. Let's learn the right ones for each relationship.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

His parents — the most important titles

PersonWhat YOU call themSound
His mom (when speaking to her)eo-meo-nim
His dad (when speaking to him)a-beo-nim
His mom (when talking ABOUT her)어머님 (same, with honorifics)same
His dad (when talking ABOUT him)아버님 (same)same

The three variants — know which is which

엄마 / 아빠 — ONLY YOUR OWN PARENTS

Casual. For YOUR own mom and dad. NEVER for his parents — sounds disrespectful and overly familiar. The "kid talking to parent" forms.

어머니 / 아버지 — STANDARD POLITE

Polite. Use for your own parents in formal contexts, or for OTHER people's parents in neutral contexts. Acceptable for his parents but 어머님/아버님 is better.

어머님 / 아버님 — HONORIFIC (USE THIS)

Adds the honorific 님. Use this for your partner's parents specifically. Signals respect + relationship. The safest choice for his mom and dad.

⚠ THE BIGGEST CULTURAL TRAP

If you accidentally call his mom 엄마 — even once, as a slip — it's the worst kind of mistake. Sounds like you're presuming to be her daughter without being married into the family.

Memory trick: YOUR parents = 엄마/아빠. HIS parents = 어머님/아버님. Never mix.

His grandparents

PersonWhat YOU call themNotes
His grandma (paternal — dad's mom)Most common
His grandpa (paternal — dad's dad)Most common
His grandma (maternal — mom's mom)Less often used face-to-face
His grandpa (maternal — mom's dad)Less often used face-to-face

The distinction between 외 (maternal) and non-외 (paternal) matters when TALKING ABOUT them to other family members. When directly addressing them, you can just say 할머님 / 할아버님 — they know which grandparent you mean from context.

Greeting his grandparents

Bow deeper for grandparents than for parents. 45° is appropriate for the first meeting with an elderly grandparent.

Note that 해요체 is acceptable for grandparents in many families (they prefer warmth to formality at their age). 하십시오체 also works if you want to be safe.

Why NEVER use 엄마 / 아빠 for his parents

엄마 (eomma, "mommy") and 아빠 (appa, "daddy") are reserved for one's own parents. They convey intimate child-parent bond. Using them for SOMEONE ELSE'S parents — without being married into the family — is presumptuous in a way that can read as either:

  • Insulting — like calling a stranger's mom "Mom" in English
  • Presumptuous — claiming the daughter-in-law role you don't have yet
  • Childishly inappropriate — using baby-talk language in formal contexts

The only exception: AFTER you marry into the family, some Korean families invite the daughter-in-law to use 엄마/아빠. But this is an explicit invitation, never an assumption. Until then (and at first meeting always): 어머님 / 아버님.

Meeting the family — the honorific titles: your boyfriend’s mother is addressed as 어머님 (eomeonim) and his father as 아버님 (abeonim) — the honorific -님 forms of mother and father, warmer and more respectful than the plain words. Using them signals you understand the relationship’s seriousness; pair them with the polite -습니다 speech level throughout the meeting.

His siblings — by age and gender

Korean sibling titles depend on TWO things: (1) the speaker's gender and (2) the sibling's age relative to the speaker. Same person, different title depending on who's calling them.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

The 4 basic sibling titles

Used byTo address older brotherTo address older sister
Female speaker (you)
Male speaker (your boyfriend)

So if your boyfriend has an older brother:

  • You (female) call him: 오빠 (oppa)
  • Your boyfriend (male) calls him: 형 (hyeong)
  • Same person, different word.

If your boyfriend has an older sister:

  • You (female) call her: 언니 (eonni)
  • Your boyfriend (male) calls her: 누나 (nuna)

Younger siblings

Korean has fewer rules for younger siblings — they're typically addressed by name or with a generic "younger sibling" word.

Younger sibling (any gender)
Younger brother specifically
Younger sister specifically

You generally call younger siblings by their first name + 씨, especially adults you don't know well:

If they're much younger or you're very close, just the name works.

When to add 님

Adding 님 to sibling titles (오빠님, 형님, etc.) is rare in casual family use — feels too formal. But there are exceptions:

  • 형님 (hyeongnim) — used by men to show respect to an older man not their actual brother (work, social). You as a female won't use this.
  • 언니 never becomes 언니님 in family use
  • 오빠 stays 오빠 even with respect
  • 누나 may become 누님 in very formal/older contexts but rare in family

For YOUR purpose (addressing your boyfriend's siblings): use the plain title — 오빠 / 언니 (depending on their gender, since you're female). No 님 needed.

The cultural meaning of 오빠 / 언니

These aren't just blood-relative words. They're used WIDELY for:

  • 오빠: any close older male (boyfriend, older male friend, older male cousin, etc.)
  • 언니: any close older female (older female friend, older female cousin, older female colleague when close, etc.)

This means when you start calling your boyfriend's older brother 오빠, you're not "stealing" your boyfriend's title — you're using a normal word that covers both. The intimate variant (오빠 for boyfriend) and the family variant (오빠 for his brother) are the same word.

💡 NAVIGATING TWO 오빠s

If your boyfriend AND his older brother are both your 오빠s, you'll often distinguish:
• Your boyfriend: just 오빠 (or 자기 in private — see Ch11)
• His brother: 첫째 오빠 ("first oppa") or use his name + 오빠: 민준 오빠 (Minjun oppa)

His family will understand from context which one you mean. Most Koreans use the name+오빠 format when multiple oppas are present.

When to switch to first name + 씨

Sometimes it's appropriate to use first name + 씨 instead of family title:

  • When his sibling is YOUNGER than you (you're the older one) — call them by name + 씨
  • When his sibling has explicitly invited "name basis" interaction
  • In professional contexts (his sister at work for example)

For an older sister (her age 28, your age 25): start with 언니. If she says "그냥 이름으로 불러도 돼" ("you can just use my name"), then transition to her name + 씨.

This is where Korean family titles get notoriously dense. English "uncle" maps to at least 4 different Korean words depending on whether it's mom's side or dad's side, married into the family or not, older or younger than the parent.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

You don't need to master all of these to make a good impression — but recognizing them helps when his family talks about each other.

💡 SHORTCUTS THAT WORK

In practice, casual conversation uses simpler versions:
• 이모 often gets used for any older female relative or even close family friend — especially among kids
• 삼촌 often gets used for any uncle informally
• When unsure, ask your boyfriend: "What do I call her?" — he'll tell you
• Adding 님 (이모님, 고모님) shows extra respect — safe with new relatives

Cousins — by relative age

Korean doesn't have a single word for "cousin." Instead, cousins are addressed by the same age-based titles used for siblings, often with a prefix:

Older male cousin (you address) or 사촌 오빠
Older female cousin (you address) or 사촌 언니
Younger cousinBy name + 씨, or 동생 / 사촌 동생

사촌 (sa-chon) means "fourth degree" — the kinship distance to a cousin. You can omit it when context is clear, but in formal introductions it specifies "cousin" rather than direct sibling.

The English-Korean mapping shortcut

Don't try to memorize all titles at once. Instead, use this practical approach:

  1. Always ask your boyfriend: "If your dad's older brother comes, what do I call him?" Get the answer once, use it.
  2. Have him write a list: who's coming to the family event + what to call each person. This is normal — Korean partners do this for each other in mixed families too.
  3. Default to safer/more formal: when unsure, add 님 (이모님 instead of 이모) or use full title + 님 (큰아버님).
  4. Smile and ask politely:

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

You don't need to act on this section yet — but knowing the landscape helps you understand Korean family conversations about other in-laws, and prepares you for what's coming if marriage happens.

What his family will call YOU after marriage

⚠ POST-MARRIAGE: TITLES CHANGE A LOT

Notice the difference: BEFORE marriage you call his younger brother by name + 씨 or 동생. AFTER marriage you call him 도련님 or 서방님 — much more formal. This formality is a tradition that signals "we are family now, with all the structure that implies."

Some modern Korean families have relaxed these titles, especially in urban Seoul. But many families still use them, especially at formal occasions (holidays, weddings, funerals). Ask your boyfriend's family about their preferences when the time comes.

The cultural weight of 며느리 (daughter-in-law)

며느리 isn't just a title — it carries cultural expectations. Traditionally (and still in many families), the daughter-in-law:

  • Helps prepare food during holidays (especially Chuseok, Lunar New Year)
  • Visits his parents' home for major holidays
  • Takes a "second daughter" role in his family
  • Often coordinates gifts/cards from your nuclear family

Modern Korean families vary widely on how much they expect from a daughter-in-law. International daughters-in-law (you) typically get extra leniency. Still, knowing the cultural baseline helps you understand what they're not asking but might appreciate.

The husband's family / the wife's family — two terms

His family (your in-laws)
Your family (his in-laws)

You'll hear these constantly in Korean discussions about married couples. When your husband says , he means his parents' house.

The 호칭 (call-name) negotiation

호칭 (ho-ching) means "what you call someone." In Korean families, especially with new in-laws, there's often an explicit conversation about which titles to use. His mom might say:

This is an invitation to use less rigid titles. Don't take it as permission to use 엄마 — but it does mean you can use less formal Korean overall.

Pet names & terms of endearment

The way Korean couples address each other tells you everything about the stage of the relationship. Here are the main pet names, what each implies, and when to use which.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

The 3 main pet names — by relationship stage

오빠 (oppa) — DATING STAGE

Used by women for boyfriends who are OLDER than them. The default Korean girlfriend term. Has been romanticized heavily by K-dramas, but is genuinely the most common term.

When to use: Once you're officially dating and he's older. Doesn't require any specific milestone.

자기 / 자기야 (jagi / jagiya) — SERIOUS COUPLE

Literally "self" — implies you and he are one. Used by both genders. The 야 suffix is a vocative (calling someone). Without it (just 자기) is also fine in conversation.

When to use: When you've been dating a while and feel solidly committed. Some couples use this from early; others wait. Following his lead is safe.

여보 (yeobo) — MARRIED ONLY

Reserved for married couples. Using it before marriage sounds presumptuous or like you're play-acting. Once married, it becomes the standard.

When to use: After marriage. Not before.

What HE might call YOU

If you're younger than him (typical with 오빠 dynamic), he might use:

Same pet name you might use for him. Common.
"Baby." Cute, can sound a bit infantilizing — depends on your taste.
"My baby." Very affectionate, often used in K-dramas.
Your name + 야 (when name ends in consonant) or 아 (vowel) — informal vocative
"Princess." Romantic, common in cuter relationships.

Names you don't want to be called (or to call him)

  • ❌ 마누라 (manura) — informal "wife." Married couples use it but it sounds rough/lower-class. Skip.
  • ❌ 남편 (nampyeon) / 아내 (anae) — "husband" / "wife." These are referential ("my husband does X") not vocative ("husband, come here"). Don't address him as 남편.
  • ❌ 오빠 if he's YOUNGER than you — only use 오빠 for older boyfriends. If he's younger, use his name + 야/아 or 자기.

The "오빠" cultural moment

💡 SAYING "오빠" — THE FIRST TIME

In K-dramas, the moment a female character switches from his name to "오빠" is depicted as romantic and significant — like the English "Can I call you my boyfriend?" milestone. In real life it's much less dramatic, but it does signal "we're a couple now."

If you're unsure about timing: just start using it. He'll either love it (most likely) or gently ask you to use his name (much less likely).

Cute speech patterns (애교, aegyo)

애교 (aegyo) is the cute, slightly childlike speech used in close relationships. It's an aesthetic choice — some couples love it, others don't. Examples:

  • Lengthening vowels: 좋아 → 조아아아 (joaaa) "good"
  • Adding ~잉 (~ing) suffix: 보고 싶어잉 (bogo sipeo-ing) "miss you~"
  • Using a higher pitch / sing-song voice
  • Saying things twice: 자기야 자기야~~

You don't need to do this. Many Korean women don't. But if your boyfriend does aegyo with you, knowing what it is helps you not be confused.

Avoiding cringe over-terms

Some pet names cross into cringe territory if overused:

  • "우리 자기야 어디 있어요?~~" (overly sweet "where is my honey?~~") — works once in a while, exhausting daily
  • Excessive aegyo voice in public — many Koreans find heavy aegyo annoying in public settings
  • Pet names with family present — never use 자기야 in front of his parents (use his name)

Public vs private register

This is important: how you address him changes by audience.

AudienceWhat to call him
Just the two of you, private오빠, 자기야, baby names — anything goes
With his close friends오빠 or just his name — they'll be used to either
With his parentsHis name only (or his name + 씨 if formal context). NEVER 자기야 / pet names in front of parents.
With his work colleagues / professional settingsHis name + 씨 (e.g., 민준 씨). Professional register.

The 잘 자 ritual

💡 GOODNIGHT TEXTS MATTER

Many Korean couples have a "goodnight" ritual — they don't sleep until they've said 잘 자 to each other. Often with hearts. If your boyfriend texts 잘 자 ❤️ before bed every night, it's a sign of a serious, caring relationship. Reciprocate:

Emoticons and stickers

Korean texting is heavy on emoticons and Kakao stickers. Common patterns:

  • ㅋㅋ at end of texts = friendly tone (a text without it can read as cold)
  • ㅎㅎ = softer, friendly
  • ~ tildes = lilting, sing-songy. 안녕~~ is friendlier than just 안녕
  • ! exclamations = enthusiasm
  • ㅠㅠ = sad / cute begging
  • Kakao stickers are integral to Korean texting — use them. There are stickers for every emotion.

Korean texting is warm and expressive by default. These can read as cold or upset, even if you didn't mean them to:

  • Just "ㅇㅇ" alone — reads as dismissive ("yeah, whatever")
  • Just "." period response — reads as upset
  • One-word responses without softeners — reads as you're busy or annoyed
  • Long delays in response without context — reads as ignoring

Fighting and making up

Every couple fights. Korean has specific scripts for how arguments unfold, how to express upset without escalating, and how to reconcile. This section is about navigating these moments without making things worse.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Expressing upset — the spectrum

Different words for "I'm upset" carry different weights. Choosing the right one matters.

서운하다 — DISAPPOINTED / HURT

Important word. Means "I feel let down" — like you expected more from him and didn't get it. NOT anger — sadness. Using this signals "we should talk about this" without escalating to a fight.

속상하다 — UPSET / DISTRESSED

Stronger than 서운하다. "Something is hurting me from the inside" — appropriate when you're really feeling it but want to express it as your pain rather than blame.

화나다 — ANGRY

Direct anger. Strong word — implies you've crossed from upset to angry. Use deliberately when something is really wrong.

The "화났어?" question

If your boyfriend senses something is off, he'll ask:

The honest, non-escalating answers:

De-escalates while still expressing the feeling
Honest minimum
Honest + opens conversation
Use only if true. If said when actually upset, it sets up a worse fight later.
⚠ THE 괜찮아 TRAP

Just like English "I'm fine" can mean "I'm NOT fine," Korean "괜찮아" (I'm fine) is sometimes used when someone is actually upset. If you're actually fine, say so clearly. If you're not, don't say 괜찮아 — say 서운해 (I'm hurt) and start the conversation. Avoiding this trap saves couples a lot of trouble.

Apologies beyond 미안

You learned 미안 / 미안해요 / 죄송합니다 in earlier chapters. For relationship apologies, you want more depth.

ApologyWeight / use
Quick, casual. For minor things.
Standard apology between couples.
Sincere — for things that mattered.
Apology + promise — for real mistakes.
The big one. Admits fault without qualification. Powerful.

The "내가 잘못했어" magic phrase

RECONCILIATION PHRASE:

Saying both — admitting fault AND apologizing — is the cultural standard for serious apologies in Korean relationships. Just "미안해" alone, without admitting fault, can feel insufficient when something really hurt the other person.

Asking for forgiveness

Accepting an apology

Standard acceptance
Forgive + reminder
Forgive but emphasize the seriousness
Generous acceptance

Reconciliation rituals

After a fight, Korean couples often have small rituals to confirm "we're okay":

  • Buying food — getting his favorite snack/dessert as a peace offering.
  • 화해 ritual (hwahae = reconciliation) — explicit "let's make up":
  • Goodnight even after fight — texting 잘 자 even on tough nights signals "we're not over, just upset"
  • Pinky promise (새끼손가락 걸기) — popular for promises to do better. Often + thumb-stamp.

What to do when you don't understand a fight

Fighting in a second language is hard. If he's upset and speaking fast, you may miss what's going on. Slow down the conversation:

If you need to switch to English to actually resolve the underlying issue, that's often OK in international couples:

This isn't a failure — it's a healthy adaptation. Many international couples switch languages during emotional conversations.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

🍜 EATING = KOREAN CULTURE

Food is central to Korean social life. Asking is the equivalent of "how are you?" Restaurants, drinking sessions, and home meals are where relationships are built and tested. This chapter covers ordering food, knowing what to order, and not embarrassing yourself at family dinners.

Getting the server's attention

In Korean restaurants, you don't passively wait — you call the server. Two main ways:

STANDARD CALL
ALTERNATIVE
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Both are perfectly polite — 저기요 is slightly more common nationwide. Speak it firmly across the restaurant. Many places now have call buttons on the tables — press them and a server comes.

💡 DON'T USE "아저씨/아주머니" UNLESS

아저씨 (mister) or 아주머니/이모 (auntie) for servers is fine in casual pojangmacha (tent bars) and traditional family-run places, but in modern restaurants 저기요 is safer. 이모 (auntie) is warm in Korean BBQ joints where there's an established "she's like family" vibe.

Ordering

The basic order pattern

Format: [dish name] + [counter, often 하나/두 개] + 주세요

For BBQ and stews ordered "per person," use 인분 (in-bun, "human-portion"). For most other dishes, 개 (counting individual items) is fine.

Specifying preferences

Non-spicy version
Less spicy
Hold an ingredient (here: cilantro)
Hold onions
For steak/BBQ — well done

Asking what's good

Asking for things during the meal

Water (most places already have water bottles on tables — refill yourself)
Side dishes are FREE and refillable — ask boldly
Extra rice (usually small cost ~1000-2000 won)
Small plate for portioning shared food
Napkins (often missing — ask!)

Requesting the bill

STANDARD
ALTERNATIVE
💡 NO TIPPING IN KOREA

Tipping is NOT done in Korean restaurants. Don't tip. Don't try to leave a tip on the table — it can confuse or even offend. The price on the menu is what you pay. (Tax and service are already included.)

Paying at the counter, not the table

In most Korean restaurants, you pay at the counter near the exit — not at your table. After saying 계산해 주세요, walk to the counter. Modern places do table-side card payment too, but counter payment is the norm.

Splitting the bill

Note: in many Korean group settings, the eldest or host pays for everyone — splitting isn't always expected. With his family, expect his parents or boyfriend to pay; offer once but don't insist.

Korean food vocabulary — the essentials

You don't need to know every dish — but recognizing the major ones lets you order, ask informed questions, and not look completely lost at his family's table.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Rice & noodle dishes

Rice bowl with veggies + meat + egg + gochujang. Tourist-favorite, family-friendly.
Korean-style rice rolls, like sushi but Korean. Cheap, fast.
Kimchi fried rice with egg on top. Classic comfort food.
Cold buckwheat noodles. Summer dish, often served after BBQ.
Simple noodle soup with light broth. Comforting.
Korean-Chinese black bean noodles. National favorite.
Spicy seafood noodle soup. Paired with jjajangmyeon at Chinese restaurants.

Stews & soups (찌개, 탕, 국)

Three different words for soup/stew, differing by thickness:

  • 찌개 (jjigae) — thick stew, usually one main ingredient
  • 탕 (tang) — clear or thicker soup, often with meat/bones
  • 국 (guk) — thin soup, light broth
Spicy kimchi stew with pork or tuna. The most common stew.
Fermented soybean stew. Earthy, not spicy. Family favorite.
Spicy soft tofu stew with egg. Hot, often comes still bubbling.
"Army stew" — spicy stew with sausage, spam, tofu, ramen. Heavy, fun.
Whole chicken stuffed with ginseng + rice in broth. Healthy summer food.
Milky ox bone soup. Mild, deeply savory.
Seaweed soup. Traditional for birthdays and new mothers.

Meat & BBQ (구이)

"Three-layer meat" — pork belly. The classic Korean BBQ.
Pork neck — leaner than samgyeopsal.
Marinated beef or pork ribs. Sweet, smoky.
Marinated beef, usually pan-cooked. Sweet, tender.
Spicy stir-fried chicken with veggies. Done at the table.
Korean fried chicken — crispy, often paired with beer (chimaek).

Other essentials

Spicy rice cakes in red sauce. Street food classic.
Korean instant ramen — different from Japanese ramen.
Savory green onion pancake. Rainy day food.
Korean dumplings, steamed or fried.
Side dishes. Always free, always refillable.

Describing taste

banmal form. Polite:
Polite: 매워요 (maewoyo)
Polite: 짜요
Polite: 달아요
Polite: 셔요 / 시어요
Polite: 써요
Polite: 기름져요
Polite: 담백해요 — used as praise
Polite: 고소해요

Asking "what is this?"

Things to avoid saying

  • ❌ "Korean food is too spicy" — even gently, sounds critical. Use "I'm still getting used to spicy food."
  • ❌ "This is weird" / "This smells weird" — about kimchi, fermented foods, sea creatures. Try first, ask questions politely.
  • ❌ "We don't eat that in America" — sounds dismissive. Better: "I haven't tried this before, what is it?"
  • ❌ Refusing without trying — at minimum take a small taste before declining more.

Table manners with his family

Eating with his family is a high-stakes performance. Specific rules — when to start, how to hold chopsticks, who serves whom. Getting these right shows you respect Korean culture. Getting them wrong is noticed (often silently).

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

The cardinal rule: WAIT for elders to start

⚠ NEVER START EATING FIRST

In Korean culture, the eldest person at the table picks up their spoon first. EVERYONE waits. This is non-negotiable at family meals. Even if you're starving, even if the food is right in front of you — wait until his dad (or whoever is the most senior elder) takes the first bite.

Watch your boyfriend's lead. He waits, you wait.

"Let's eat" — the two phrases

Before eating (after the eldest starts):

BEFORE EATING — formal

Said to the cook/host before starting. Like "bon appétit" but spoken BY the eater. Slight bow as you say it.

AFTER EATING — formal

Said to the cook/host after finishing. Match with a slight bow. Don't leave the table without saying this.

Polite versions (해요체): — fine for friends, but with his parents use 하십시오체.

Chopsticks rules

RuleWhy
Never stick chopsticks upright in riceResembles incense at funerals. Major taboo.
Don't pass food from chopstick to chopstickResembles bone-picking ritual at cremation. Put food on a plate first.
Don't stab food with chopsticksConsidered crude.
Lay chopsticks across the bowl or on the chopstick rest when not usingDon't leave them sticking out.
Use the spoon for rice, chopsticks for everything elseKorean style — different from Chinese/Japanese. Rice is shoveled with spoon, side dishes picked with chopsticks.
Hold the bowl on the table — don't lift itUnlike Japan/China. Korean rice bowl stays on the table; you bring spoon to mouth, not bowl.

Pace and quantity

  • Eat at the elders' pace. Don't finish dramatically before everyone else. Don't lag dramatically behind.
  • Try a bit of everything. Refusing entire dishes can offend the cook. Take small portions if unsure.
  • Don't leave food on your plate. Take only what you'll eat. Korean meals have many small dishes — sample, don't mountain-pile.
  • You don't have to finish rice if you're full. Saying is fine — but make it clear you ate well first.

Serving others — the two-hand rule

💡 THE TWO-HAND RULE FOR ELDERS

When pouring drinks, serving food, or passing anything to an elder, use BOTH HANDS. Either both hands on the bottle/dish, or one hand on the object and the other lightly touching your opposite forearm or wrist.

This applies to: pouring drinks, passing the salt, refilling water, handing them anything. Single-handed gestures to elders read as careless or rude.

Pouring drinks

You'll often need to refill his parents' drinks (water, soju, beer). Rules:

  1. Notice when their glass is empty. Don't wait to be asked — refill proactively.
  2. Hold the bottle with both hands, or one hand on the bottle + other hand lightly on your forearm.
  3. Pour from a respectful distance, not splashing.
  4. Don't refill your OWN glass — wait for someone to pour for you. (Pouring your own is a tiny faux pas — minor but noticed.)

Receiving food / drink from an elder

When his mom serves you food onto your plate, or his dad pours you a drink — receive with both hands. The receiving gesture:

  • Both hands on the glass/plate as you accept
  • Or one hand receiving + other hand touching your forearm/wrist
  • A small with a slight head bow

The "한 그릇 더?" (one more bowl?) ritual

Korean moms famously over-serve. After your first bowl, his mom will ask:

Or simply:

Honest answers:

Accept with limit. Good middle ground.
Polite decline. Add a compliment.
The diplomatic decline. Praises the food + explains.

End of meal

When everyone's done:

  1. Say with a small bow
  2. Offer to help clear the table:
  3. His mom will likely say "no, just sit" — offer one or two more times, then accept (see Ch13 for the full ritual)

Drinking culture (술자리)

술자리 (suljari) literally means "alcohol place" — refers to any drinking gathering. Korean drinking culture has its own elaborate rules. Even if you don't drink, knowing the rules helps you understand what's happening and decline gracefully.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

The main drinks

National drink. Cheap, ubiquitous. Green bottles.
Beer. Often mixed with soju to make 소맥 (somaek).
Traditional rice wine. Lower alcohol, slightly sweet.
Wine — increasingly popular at family meals.

Pouring rules — for elders

When pouring soju/beer for his father or an elder:

  1. Hold the bottle with BOTH HANDS — right hand on the bottle, left hand lightly under your right elbow or on your right wrist
  2. Pour slowly, fill to about 80% (not to the top)
  3. Wait until they pick up their glass before pouring — they may extend it toward you to receive

Receiving a drink from an elder

This happens constantly. His dad picks up the soju bottle and pours for you. Rules:

  1. Hold your glass with BOTH HANDS as he pours — right hand on glass, left hand supporting underneath
  2. Don't move your glass while he's pouring
  3. Small bow / nod as you accept:

Drinking with elders — the turn-head rule

⚠ THE HEAD-TURN RULE

When drinking in front of elders, turn your head AWAY from them as you drink. Bring the glass to your mouth, turn your head 45-90° to the side (away from the eldest person), drink, then return.

This is centuries-old respect protocol. Drinking directly facing an elder (especially making eye contact) is considered confrontational or disrespectful.

Cover the glass with your free hand as you drink for extra deference.

The 건배 (cheers) ritual

Before the first drink of any toast:

When clinking glasses with an elder, hold your glass LOWER than theirs (rim of your glass below rim of theirs). This is the visual equivalent of bowing — signals you defer.

Refilling rules

  • Don't refill your own glass. Wait for someone to pour for you. (Refilling your own is the small "no one cares about me" gesture — minor but noticed.)
  • Watch others' glasses. When his dad's glass empties, refill it (with both hands) before he asks.
  • Don't refill if there's still drink in the glass — wait until almost empty.

Politely refusing alcohol

Many Koreans (especially traditional families) consider it impolite to refuse a drink from an elder. But there are graceful ways:

DON'T DRINK ALCOHOL AT ALL

Direct. State it clearly. Add a reason if you want: 알레르기가 있어요 (I have an allergy) or 약 먹고 있어요 (I'm taking medication).

DRINK LIGHTLY / SLOWLY

Accept a tiny pour, sip slowly. You don't have to finish each glass.

ACCEPT FIRST POUR, DECLINE REFILLS

A "I'm pacing myself" signal. Polite and culturally readable.

The "원샷" (one shot) thing

원샷 (wonsyat, "one shot") means drink the glass in one go. Korean drinking culture sometimes pressures this — especially at company dinners (회식). With family it's much rarer, but possible at celebrations.

If pressured:

The "I've had enough" phrases

Polite "I'm done"
Self-deprecating decline. Often gets a laugh + accepted.
Soft close — "today" implies "next time maybe more"

What if you DO get drunk

If alcohol gets the better of you with family — first time, especially — it can be embarrassing. Mitigation:

  • Eat as you drink. Korean drinking is paired with anju (안주, drinking snacks) for a reason.
  • Drink water between rounds. Pour yourself water from the table bottle (this you CAN do yourself).
  • If feeling too drunk: step outside for fresh air, or apologize and excuse yourself:
  • Next morning text: if you embarrassed yourself, send a brief apology to his mom via your boyfriend:

End of Chapter 12

  • ✓ Call servers with 저기요 / 여기요
  • ✓ Order with [dish] + [number] 주세요, ask for sides/water/bill
  • ✓ Recognize the major Korean dishes (찌개 vs 탕 vs 국, BBQ types, rice/noodle dishes)
  • ✓ WAIT for elders to start eating
  • ✓ Say 잘 먹겠습니다 before, 잘 먹었습니다 after
  • ✓ Avoid chopstick taboos (no upright in rice, no chopstick-to-chopstick)
  • ✓ Two-hand rule for serving/receiving with elders
  • ✓ Turn head when drinking in front of elders
  • ✓ Pour for others, never refill your own glass
  • ✓ Decline drinks gracefully if needed

🧹 HELPING = HUGE POINTS

In Korean families, the daughter-in-law's helpfulness at the house is watched (sometimes obsessively). You DON'T have to actually do the work — but you absolutely must OFFER. The ritual matters more than the labor. This chapter covers offering, handling the polite refusal, and what to actually do when accepted.

The 3-time offer rule

💡 OFFER, OFFER, OFFER AGAIN

Korean politeness often requires the host to refuse help the first 1-2 times, even if they'd appreciate help. The protocol is: offer 2-3 times before accepting "no." If you only offer once and accept the polite refusal, you came across as having "checked the box" rather than genuinely wanting to help.

Volunteering to help

The opening offer

SAFE STANDARD OFFER

The humble verb 드리다 ("to give to a superior") makes this respectful. Use this as your default offer.

WHAT CAN I DO?
SPECIFIC OFFER

Specific offers can be more powerful — shows you noticed what needed doing. 설거지 = dishes.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

The polite refusal you'll hear

Almost certainly, his mom will refuse the first offer. Common refusals:

"Just sit" — banmal version
Polite refusal
"You're a guest" reasoning
Deferring to a future visit

The 2nd and 3rd offers

After the polite refusal, OFFER AGAIN — gently, not pushy. Two more rounds:

Second offer

The "어머님 좀 쉬세요" (please rest a bit) frames the help as concern for HER, not just chores.

Third offer (if she refuses twice)

"제가 하고 싶어서요" = "because I want to" — frames it as your desire, removing the obligation framing.

When she finally accepts

If she says yes (often on the 2nd or 3rd offer), she might say:

Or:

Respond enthusiastically:

When the offer ISN'T accepted

Sometimes — even after 3 offers — she truly wants you to sit. In that case, accept gracefully:

The commitment to NEXT time keeps you on the helpful track. It also tells her you genuinely wanted to.

Things you can usually offer even if refused

Some small helpful gestures are accepted even from "guests":

  • Clearing your own plate — almost never refused. Take your dishes to the sink area without asking.
  • Wiping the table — small, low-stakes
  • Pouring drinks for others at the table
  • Helping serve food onto plates if dishes are being passed around

What NOT to do

  • ❌ Don't aggressively insist on doing chores after a clear "no." Pushing past 3 offers can feel like you're questioning her hospitality.
  • ❌ Don't reorganize her kitchen — even with helpful intent. Don't move things around or "tidy" without instruction.
  • ❌ Don't make a big show of helping — quiet, steady effort is better than performative announcement.
  • ❌ Don't volunteer to cook on your first visit (unless explicitly invited). The kitchen is her domain.

Compliments on the food

Complimenting his mom's cooking is one of the most important things you can do. The right compliments win serious affection points; flat ones miss the chance.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

The basic compliment

SIMPLE / STANDARD
EMPHATIC
STRONGER

Going beyond "맛있어요" — specific compliments

Generic "delicious" is fine but forgettable. Specific praise lands much harder.

Naming the dish makes it specific
시원하다 for soup = high praise. Literally "cool" but for soup means "clean, clearing" — a hangover-cure quality.
Praising specific quality (tender meat)
HUGE compliment — means salt/spice is perfectly balanced
Express genuine novelty and appreciation

The "best ___ I've ever had" formulation

Substitute the dish name. Format: 제가 먹어 본 [dish] 중에 제일 맛있어요 = "of all the [dishes] I've eaten, this is the most delicious."

Giving compliments

Korean compliments have specific phrasings and a tone different from English. Direct English-style "I love your dress!" can land flat or wrong. Knowing the right verbs and patterns makes compliments land warmly.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

The three main compliment verbs

멋있다 — cool / impressive / sharp

Universal compliment. Works for clothes, hairstyle, skills, accomplishments. Slightly more masculine but used for everyone.

예쁘다 — pretty / beautiful

For appearance, decorations, things. Used for women, children, flowers, dress. NOT used for men's appearance (use 잘생기다 — handsome — for men).

잘하다 — skilled / does well

For skills and abilities — cooking, singing, language, work. The honorific 시 makes it polite when complimenting someone older or superior.

Specific compliment patterns

Complimenting appearance (women)

Praising her outfit
Praising hair
Universal good compliment for any woman
Small face is considered very attractive — well-received compliment

Complimenting appearance (men)

"Handsome" — use this for men, NOT 예뻐요

Tall = positive in Korean culture

Complimenting cooking

Complimenting work / accomplishments

For achievements — getting a degree, a job, finishing something hard
Praising competence
"I'm proud" — strong intimate compliment (boyfriend, close family)

Awkward direct translations to AVOID

  • ❌ "You look young" — translates as 어려 보여요 (eoryeo boyeoyo). Actually FINE in Korean — telling someone they look young is positive at any age. So this one's safe to use!
  • ❌ "You look great today" direct translation (오늘 좋아 보여요) — actually OK but vague; more specific is better.
  • ❌ "Your English is so good!" to a Korean person — many find this backhanded ("why wouldn't it be?"). Don't praise their English unless they specifically struggled.
  • ❌ "You look like a celebrity" to his mom or dad — usually too forward.
  • ❌ "You're so funny" directly translated (재밌어요) to elders — can sound diminishing. Better: "이야기 정말 재밌게 하시네요" ("you tell stories really interestingly").

Compliment intensity ladder

From soft to strong:

  1. 맛있어요 — it's delicious (basic)
  2. 너무 맛있어요 — it's so delicious (emphatic)
  3. 정말 맛있어요 — it's really delicious (stronger)
  4. 진짜 너무 맛있어요 — it's really so delicious (very strong)
  5. 이렇게 맛있는 거 처음이에요 — I've never tasted anything this delicious (max)

Same pattern works with 예뻐요, 멋있어요, 잘하시네요, etc.

The "honorific compliment" pattern

When complimenting elders specifically, add the honorific 시 to most compliments:

To peer: 잘해요To elder: 잘하시네요
To peer: 예뻐요To elder: 예쁘세요
To peer: 좋아요To elder: 좋으세요
To peer: 멋있어요To elder: 멋있으세요

The ~시네요 ending (with 네 — "I see/notice") is especially good for compliments because it sounds like genuine observation rather than flattery.

Receiving compliments — the humility script

Korean culture has a strict ritual for accepting compliments. The American "thank you!" — accepting the compliment as your due — sounds borderline arrogant in Korean. You MUST deflect first. Knowing this script is critical for interacting with his family.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

The core deflection: 아니에요

DEFAULT DEFLECTION

Said with a small wave of the hand and a slight head-shake. Means "not at all." The compliment-deflection equivalent of "please" in English.

STRONGER DEFLECTION

Doubling shows you really mean it — appropriate for stronger compliments.

The expanded deflection patterns

Deflect + minimize
For skill compliments — "still learning"
"I'm embarrassed" — endearing deflection
Formal/honorific — "you flatter me"

Compliment-specific deflections

If they compliment your Korean

If they compliment your appearance

If they compliment your cooking

Bonus move: deflect + COMPLIMENT THEM BACK. This is doubly culturally correct.

If they compliment your work / studies

"All thanks to others" — the ultimate Korean humility — credits the achievement to others (mentors, family, team).

When to STOP deflecting and accept

If you deflect 1-2 times and they keep insisting on the compliment, eventually accept gracefully:

Or simply:

"I'll work even harder" — promise of future effort — is the Korean way to receive a compliment without sounding arrogant. You're saying "thank you, but I'm still working at it."

The body language

  • Hand wave (small, in front of chest): the standard "no no" gesture
  • Head shake (small, side to side): can accompany 아니에요
  • Slight bow / head dip: when accepting a compliment
  • Slight smile, not big grin: when receiving — too much smile reads as enjoying the praise
  • Hand to chest / heart: when very moved by a compliment

The wrong way (avoid)

What sounds wrong in Korean even though it's natural English:

  • ❌ "Thank you, I know!" or "Yes, isn't it?" — agreeing with the compliment = arrogance.
  • ❌ "Thanks!" with no deflection — accepting at face value = mildly arrogant.

Special case: compliments from his mom

His mom may compliment you constantly — your dress, your manners, your Korean. Be especially careful to deflect. With his mom:

  1. Always deflect first (아니에요)
  2. Often add a compliment back to her (그건 어머님께서 잘 가르쳐 주신 덕분이에요 = "that's thanks to your good teaching")
  3. Then if she insists, accept gracefully with 감사합니다

Mutual deflection-then-reciprocal-compliment is the cultural dance. Both parties leave feeling good.

Returning favors and gifts

Korean gift and favor culture is reciprocal. Receiving without ever returning creates social debt. The cycle of give-and-give-back is part of how relationships are maintained.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order

The "first refuse, then accept" ritual

You learned this for help (Ch13) and food (Ch13). Same applies to gifts.

When his mom hands you a gift

First refusal:

Second refusal:

Then accept (with both hands):

NEVER refuse 3+ times. Past 2 polite refusals, accepting graciously is the right move.

Reciprocation principles

💡 RECIPROCATION HAPPENS

Korean culture has a strong norm of returning favors — but with TIMING and APPROPRIATENESS. Not immediately (that'd look transactional), but eventually, in proportion.

Timing of reciprocation

  • Same day: Don't reciprocate same-day for major gifts (looks like balancing a ledger). Verbal thanks is enough.
  • Within weeks: If she gave you a gift on visit 1, bring a thoughtful gift on visit 2.
  • Annually: Korean holidays (Seollal, Chuseok) are natural reciprocation points — see Ch22.
  • Major occasions: Her birthday, her parents' birthdays = chances to return.

Proportionality

Don't return a $50 gift with a $200 gift — that signals "I owe you nothing now." Match approximately, or slightly less. The thought matters more than the size.

Specific reciprocation contexts

She gives you take-home food

Wash and return the containers on your next visit. Bringing them filled with something small (a snack, a small bottle of juice) is a graceful return.

She gives you money envelopes

No need to return cash. Instead, on the next visit bring a thoughtful gift — fruit basket, supplements, something nice for her or his dad. The cash gift was hers to give; your return is care, not equivalence.

She helps you with something big

(Driving you somewhere, finding you a doctor, etc.) — verbal thanks immediately, then a small gift (cake, flowers) within a week or two.

The "신세 졌어요" — I owe you

An important phrase when receiving substantial help:

Formal version:

Saying this is acknowledging that you'll repay/return eventually. It's a relationship-builder, not a transaction.

What NOT to do

  • ❌ Don't make a big show of paying back. "Here, this is to make up for the gift" reads transactional/cold.
  • ❌ Don't over-reciprocate in size — feels like rejection of her care.
  • ❌ Don't reciprocate within hours/same day. The pause is part of acknowledgment.
  • ❌ Don't forget entirely. Korean families track these things; long-term reciprocation matters.
  • ❌ Don't reciprocate with money (unless she gave money for a specific purpose).

The "I'll return the favor" closer

After receiving major help/gifts, end your thanks with a promise to return:

Casual promise
Promise of future effort
For major help — heartfelt

Compliments and gifts pulled together

Real-life scenario at his mom's house — full sequence:

  1. She compliments your outfit: "옷이 예쁘네"
  2. You deflect + compliment her back: "아니에요, 어머님이 더 잘 입으세요"
  3. She insists: "진짜 잘 어울려"
  4. You accept gracefully: "감사합니다" with small bow
  5. Later she gives you a small gift (a scarf): you refuse twice then accept with both hands + "정말 감사합니다, 잘 쓰겠습니다"
  6. On the next visit, you bring her something thoughtful (specialty tea, a small gift from your trip, etc.)

This whole flow takes ~30 seconds in real life but signals everything: respect, humility, reciprocity, ongoing relationship.
